#### 12.3.3 International Resources Applicable to Chemical Hazards

The CAC was formed in 1963 to develop food standards, guidelines, and related texts such as
Codes of Practice, and is recognized under the World Trade Organization Agreement on the
Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (SPS Agreement) as the international
standards organization for food safety. The CAC receives scientific advice in reports from
standing and ad hoc committees. These documents could be helpful resources in supporting
decisions made in your hazard analysis (including decisions about whether the chemical hazard
could be managed through CGMPs) as well as your identification and implementation of
preventive controls for a chemical hazard in your food, particularly if FDA has not provided
relevant information for that chemical hazard-food pair. \[12\]
See Table 6 in section VI of the Introduction of this guidance for those international documents
(such as Codes of Practice) that are most relevant to the prevention and reduction of chemical
contaminants in food. For example, these Codes of Practice provide recommendations for the
prevention and/or reduction of chemical contaminants such as acrylamide, arsenic, cadmium,
lead, 3-MCPDE, and GE, and mycotoxins (such as aflatoxin, deoxynivalenol (DON), and
ochratoxin) in certain foods. These Codes of Practice could supplement guidances and other
information FDA has provided with respect to supporting measures (such as preventive
controls) that significantly minimize or prevent chemical hazards.
See Table 6 in section VI of the Introduction of this guidance for the Codex General Standard
for Contaminants and Toxicants in Food and Feed, CXS 193-1995. This general standard may
be helpful for use as a guide for determining your specifications for levels of chemical
contaminants in foods when FDA has not established a contaminant level for a particular
chemical contaminant in a particular food or group of foods. Importantly, a contaminant level for
a particular chemical contaminant in a particular food or group of foods established by FDA is
the relevant contaminant level rather than a maximum level (ML) established by the CAC.

#### 12.3.4 Factors to Consider in Evaluating Whether a Known or Reasonably Foreseeable (“Potential”) Chemical Hazard Can Be Effectively Managed Through Application of CGMPs or Is a Hazard Requiring a Preventive Control

Following CGMPs is sometimes called a “prerequisite program” (NACMCF, 1998) to signify that
the measures that you take to comply with the CGMP requirements should be in place before
you conduct your hazard analysis and identify risk-based preventive controls to address specific
hazards. The preventive controls that you identify and implement to control chemical hazards
should complement and enhance the measures you have in place to comply with the CGMP
requirements to protect against contamination of food with chemical hazards. CGMP measures
can be enhanced by the addition of preventive control management components to function as
a preventive control.
Your hazard analysis should consider which known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”)
hazards can be effectively managed through the application of CGMPs and other prerequisite
programs, and which hazards require one or more preventive controls. Factors that you should
consider during your hazard analysis include:
12 Reference to these documents is provided for informational purposes only. These documents are not
incorporated by reference into this guidance and are not FDA guidance.

- information about the known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”) hazards;
- information about the food and the production process, including:
`o` association of the type of food with illness or injury due to the hazard (e.g., outbreaks or
recalls associated with the food);
`o` the sources of raw materials and other ingredients (e.g., knowledge or experience with a
supplier’s history and performance);
`o` information about the manufacturing process, including:
  - formulation of the food;
  - handling of the food during production;
  - the condition, function, and design of the facility and equipment;
  - the steps followed to prepare the finished product, the control measures applied
  during those steps, and the impact of those control measures on the hazard; and
  - the reasonably foreseeable use of the food, including consumption by vulnerable
  populations; and
  `o` the PCQI’s judgement about whether and how control of the hazard would benefit from
  preventive control management components (i.e., monitoring, corrective actions and
  corrections, verification, and associated records);
- the probability that a known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”) hazard will occur in the
absence of preventive controls, which may be informed by:
`o` knowledge of the history of the production of the food at the facility, e.g., past lapses \[13\] in
the application of control measures (such as CGMPs or other prerequisite programs);
`o` testing results related to identification of a hazard in the food;
`o` an understanding of actions taken to comply with other applicable requirements, such
as:
  - USDA’s marketing orders pertaining to mold in general, or mycotoxin hazards in
  particular, in several RACs; and
  - regulations issued by FDA’s Center for Veterinary Medicine (CVM) pertaining to
  chemical hazards in feed for food-producing animals; and
  `o` an understanding of participation in programs such as:
  - the Grade “A” Pasteurized Milk Ordinance (PMO) under the FDA program of the
  National Conference on Interstate Milk Shipments (NCIMS) pertaining to chemical
  hazards in dairy products; and
  - USDA’s voluntary programs for grading grain RACs relevant to quality defects,
  including those consistent with a higher probability of mycotoxin presence (e.g.,
  mold-, insect- or weather-damaged kernels); and
- the severity of the illness or injury if the hazard were to occur.
During reanalysis of your food safety plan in accordance with 21 CFR 117.170, we recommend
that you consider any regulatory action by FDA (e.g., regarding contaminant levels) that could
lead to changes in the specifications that you set for contaminants and whether such changes
impact your evaluation of which known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”) hazards can be
13 Measures that you could use to assess past lapses in the application of CGMP measures include the
frequency of reprocessing, reworking, diverting to a use that does not present a safety concern, or
destroying the food and the frequency of product recalls.

effectively managed through the application of CGMPs and other prerequisite programs, and
which hazards require one or more preventive controls.

#### 12.3.5 Evaluating Environmental Contaminants

Environmental contaminants (such as toxic elements (e.g., arsenic, cadmium, and lead),
dioxins, perchlorates, PFAS, and radionuclides) generally are geographically localized as a
result of natural occurrence, industrial contamination, or accidental release during or following a
natural or industrial disaster.
We recommend that you address environmental contaminants through avoidance whenever
possible. For example, you should be able to avoid sourcing food ingredients from
geographically localized sites that have been contaminated following a natural or industrial
disaster or as a result of limited industrial contamination (e.g., industrial contamination that
affected a limited geographic area). When the location of these sites is well known, you could
avoid sourcing an ingredient from the affected areas without identifying the environmental
contaminant as a hazard requiring a supply-chain program as a preventive control.
In some cases, environmental contaminants are present over a relatively wide geographic area
due to natural occurrence and ongoing industrial contamination, including contamination from
multiple sources. For example, this is the case for toxic elements in some areas where RACs
are grown. In evaluating whether an environmental contaminant in a RAC used as an ingredient
could be a hazard requiring a preventive control, we recommend that you consider:

- the factors we identified in section 12.3.4; and
- the intended consumer. A priority for FDA is reducing dietary exposure to contaminants to
as low as possible, while maintaining access to nutritious food (see our Closer to Zero
website, Table 8 in section VI of the Introduction of this guidance). FDA has prioritized foods
commonly eaten by babies and young children because their smaller body sizes and
metabolism make them more vulnerable to the harmful effects of these contaminants. If you
manufacture foods intended for babies and young children, we recommend that you identify
applicable toxic elements that are known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”) hazards in
ingredients of such foods as hazards requiring a supply-chain program as a preventive
control. See sections 12.10 and 12.11 for examples of how to do so.

#### 12.3.6 Evaluating Natural Toxins

The PCHF requirements specify that you must consider, as part of your hazard identification,
known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”) chemical hazards that include natural toxins (see
21 CFR 117.130(b)(1)(ii)).

##### 12.3.6.1 Evaluating mycotoxins

Mycotoxins are toxic metabolites produced by molds that can infect and proliferate on RACs
such as grains (e.g., wheat and corn), peanuts, fruits, and tree nuts in the field and during
storage. Mycotoxin hazards are generally addressed through a combination of modern
agricultural and processing practices, particularly during storage (on farms and in food
processing facilities). For several RACs, marketing orders established by USDA’s Agricultural
Marketing Service (AMS) include provisions to assess the potential presence of mold in general

or aflatoxin in particular and restrict the marketing of commodities that do not satisfy moldrelated criteria or aflatoxin-related criteria in the marketing order. For example:

- For domestic and imported peanuts marketed in the United States, the marketing order in 7
CFR part 996 includes outgoing quality standards for shelled peanuts (see 7 CFR 996.31)
requiring results certified as “negative” for aflatoxin following laboratory analysis before
shipping or otherwise disposing of shelled peanuts for human consumption.
- Marketing orders and import regulations applicable to pistachios do not allow shipment for
domestic human consumption of pistachios that exceed a specified aflatoxin level and
require all shipments to be covered by an aflatoxin inspection certificate (see 7 CFR
983.150 for “aflatoxin regulations” for pistachios grown in California, Arizona, and New
Mexico and 7 CFR 999.600 for import regulations applicable to aflatoxin in imported
pistachios).
- For almonds grown in California, the marketing order in 7 CFR part 981 includes a definition
(see 7 CFR 981.8) for an inedible kernel, in part, as a kernel, piece, or particle of almond
kernel with any defect scored as damage due to mold. Additional provisions of 7 CFR part
981 establish quality control requirements for determining and disposing of inedible kernels
(see 7 CFR 981.42 and 981.442).
- For hazelnuts grown in Oregon and Washington, the marketing order in 7 CFR part 982
includes grade requirements (see 7 CFR 982.101) specifying that hazelnut kernels or
portions of hazelnut kernels must be free from mold.
For grains, applicable control measures include collection of samples for evaluation of grain
quality and for the potential for contamination with mycotoxins. The Federal Grain Inspection
Service (FGIS) of the USDA AMS sets standards for U.S. grain grades and grade requirements
and oversees a voluntary (fee-for-service) national inspection system applicable to grains (see 7
CFR part 810). \[14\] Grades and grade requirements for grains address defects that are consistent
with a higher probability of mycotoxin presence (such as the presence of kernels that have been
damaged by mold, insects, or weather). Under the voluntary national inspection system, food
producers can request grading of grain and specify a certain grade in purchase agreements. For
example, U.S. No. 1 grade wheat has the lowest maximum percent limits for damaged kernels
(see 7 CFR 810.2204). In addition, under the authority of the United States Grains Standards
Act (7 U.S.C. 71-87k), as amended, and the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 (7 U.S.C. 16211627), as amended, AMS provides official mycotoxin testing services throughout the United
States for domestic and export grains, oilseeds, and processed-grain commodities. Official
testing services are provided for aflatoxins, DON, fumonisins, ochratoxin A, and zearalenone. \[15\]
14 See also “Overview of U.S. Wheat Inspection,” a booklet printed in 2021 by U.S. Wheat Associates in
cooperation with USDA/AMS/FGIS to provide information on the national, official grain inspection and
weighing system used in the United States. Available at
[https://www.uswheat.org/wp-content/uploads/Overview-of-U.S.-Wheat-Inspection.pdf.](https://www.uswheat.org/wp-content/uploads/Overview-of-U.S.-Wheat-Inspection.pdf)
15 Testing at field locations requires rapid, inexpensive, and accurate methods to effectively assess U.S.
grain quality. An essential part of ensuring the quality of official mycotoxin testing is the AMS test kit
evaluation program, through which test kits are evaluated and certified for conformance to specific
criteria. Only test kits having AMS certification are approved for official mycotoxin testing. AMS
establishes the test kit performance criteria and periodically updates them to improve testing accuracy
and to meet the official mycotoxin testing program's operational needs (87 FR 67859, November 10,
2022).

In evaluating whether a mycotoxin hazard in a RAC ingredient could be a hazard requiring a
preventive control, we recommend that you consider factors such as the factors we identified in
section 12.3.4.

##### 12.3.6.2 Evaluating plant-produced toxins

Some plants naturally produce toxins. For example, the toxin hypoglycin A is found at high
levels in the unripe fruit of the tropical ackee tree. Ingestion of hypoglycin A may result in no
symptoms or symptoms that range from mild (e.g., some vomiting) to severe (e.g., vomiting with
profound hypoglycemia, drowsiness, muscular exhaustion, prostration, and possibly coma and
death). When ackee is fully ripe, the hypoglycin A drops to negligible levels in the fruit (other
than the rind and seeds, which should not be consumed). If the fruit is not properly processed,
the finished product could contain more than a negligible level of hypoglycin A and could pose a
health risk. In a CPG issued in 2014, FDA determined that canned ackee, frozen ackee, or other
ackee products containing concentrations of hypoglycin A above 100 ppm have not been
processed properly and that finished product may be injurious to health. For more information
about the processing of ackee, see our CPG 550.050 Canned Ackee, Frozen Ackee, and Other
Ackee Products – Hypoglycin A Toxin (see Table 3 in section VI of the Introduction of this
guidance). As discussed in that CPG, key control measures for hypoglycin A begin with
selection of fruit that is ripe, followed by removal of rind, seeds, and raphe before processing.
In evaluating whether a plant-produced toxin in an ingredient could be a hazard requiring a
preventive control, we recommend that you consider the factors we identified in section 12.3.4.

#### 12.3.7 Evaluating Pesticide Residues

The PCHF requirements specify that you must consider, as part of your hazard identification,
known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”) chemical hazards that include pesticide residues
(see 21 CFR 117.130(b)(1)(ii)). Pesticide residues could be present in food crops and in foods
of animal origin (e.g., as a result of pesticide residues in animal food) (see draft Chapter 3). The
U.S. EPA registers the use of pesticides and may establish tolerances for pesticide chemical
residues that could remain in or on food (see 40 CFR part 180). A detailed description of how
FDA enforces pesticide tolerances in human and animal food is available in our 1995 CPG Sec.
575.100 Pesticide Residues in Food and Feed – Enforcement Criteria \[16\] (see Table 3 in section
VI of the Introduction of this guidance) and on FDA’s pesticide monitoring website (see Table 8
in section VI of the Introduction of this guidance) \[17\] . FDA monitors levels of pesticide residues in
the U.S. food supply and publishes an annual report summarizing the findings from this
monitoring each year (see Table 8 in section VI of the Introduction of this guidance).
16 The regulation of food containing pesticide chemical residues is governed by sections 201, 402, and
408 of the FD&C Act) (21 U.S.C. 321, 342, and 346a, respectively). These sections of the FD&C Act were
amended by the passage of the Food Quality Protection Act of 1996 (FQPA, Pub. Law 104–107). In
2008, FDA issued as draft guidance a revised CPG Sec. 575.100 that, when finalized, will represent
FDA’s current thinking on enforcement criteria for pesticide residues in food and feed, taking into account
the provisions of the FQPA.
17 See also our 2009 Memorandum of Understanding with USDA (FSIS and AMS) and EPA regarding
regulatory activities concerning residues of drugs, pesticides, and environmental contaminants in foods
(MOU 225-85-8400). Available at
[https://www.fda.gov/AboutFDA/PartnershipsCollaborations/MemorandaofUnderstandingMOUs/Domestic](https://www.fda.gov/AboutFDA/PartnershipsCollaborations/MemorandaofUnderstandingMOUs/DomesticMOUs/ucm116368.htm)
[MOUs/ucm116368.htm.](https://www.fda.gov/AboutFDA/PartnershipsCollaborations/MemorandaofUnderstandingMOUs/DomesticMOUs/ucm116368.htm)

In evaluating whether a pesticide hazard in a food ingredient could be a hazard requiring a
preventive control, we recommend that you consider:

- the factors we identified in section 12.3.4; and
- whether the food has a history of violative pesticide residues. For commodities associated
with violative pesticide residues in domestic and imported foods, see:
`o` U.S. Food and Drug Administration regulatory pesticide residue monitoring of human
foods: 2009-2017, Food Additives & Contaminants: Part A (Liang et al., 2021);
`o` FDA’s Pesticide Residue Monitoring Program Reports and Data (Table 8 in section VI of
the Introduction);
`o` Import Alert 99-05 Detention Without Physical Examination of Raw Agricultural Products
for Pesticides (which applies to specific growers) (Table 5 in section VI of the
Introduction \[18\] );
`o` Import Alert 99-08 Detention without Physical Examination of Processed Human and
Animal Foods for Pesticides (which applies to specific commercial entities) (Table 5 in
section VI of the Introduction);
`o` Import Alert 99-14 Countrywide Detention Without Physical Examination of Raw
Agricultural Products for Pesticides (which applies to countries rather than to specific
commercial entities) (Table 5 in section VI of the Introduction); and
`o` Import Alert 99-15 (Countrywide Detention Without Physical Examination of Processed
Foods for Pesticides) (Table 5 in section VI of the Introduction).

#### 12.3.8 Evaluating Residues of Animal Drugs

The PCHF requirements specify that you must consider, as part of your hazard identification,
known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”) chemical hazards that include drug residues (see
21 CFR 117.130(b)(1)(ii)). A hazard analysis for drug residues should consider factors such as
whether a tolerance has been established for the particular drug-food combination, and whether
a tolerance level has been exceeded (see draft Chapter 3). Animal drugs used according to
label directions, regulations, and veterinary directives should not result in residues that exceed
the tolerances established for the drugs in animal-derived food products such as meat, milk, or
egg products. Note that extra-label uses of certain drugs (e.g., the use of antibiotics such as
chloramphenicol, nitrofuran drugs, or fluoroquinolone drugs in honeybees) are prohibited for
therapeutic purposes and only allowed in narrow circumstances. \[19\] Such antibiotics have been
detected in honey and blended syrup products (see Import Alert 36-04).
In evaluating whether a drug residue in an animal-derived ingredient could be a hazard requiring
a preventive control, we recommend that you consider:

- the factors we identified in section 12.3.4; and
18 Table 5 in the draft Introduction that we made available for public comment in 2024 did not include
Import Alerts 99-05, 99-08, 99-14, and 99-15. We intend to include these import alerts in that table when
we next update the Introduction. To find a list of FDA import alerts, please visit Search for Import Alerts at
[https://www.fda.gov/industry/import-alerts/search-import-alerts](https://www.fda.gov/industry/import-alerts/search-import-alerts).
19 See 21 CFR 530.21, 530.25, and 530.41.
- Import Alert 36-04 Detention Without Physical Examination of Honey and Blended Syrup
Due to Unsafe Drug Residues.

#### 12.3.9 Evaluating Unapproved Food Additives or Color Additives

The PCHF requirements specify that you must consider, as part of your hazard identification,
known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”) chemical hazards that include unapproved food
additives or color additives (see 21 CFR 117.130(b)(1)(ii)). See draft Chapter 3 for a discussion
of the statutory framework for lawful use of food ingredients. Generally, the safety of food
ingredients is established under specific conditions of use, such as a maximum level of use or
use only in certain food categories, before the ingredients are used in the manufacturing or
processing of human food in accordance with part 117. With certain exceptions, substances
used in the manufacturing or processing of food that are not authorized for their use as food
additives by FDA or are not generally recognized by qualified experts as safe (GRAS) for their
use (as demonstrated through either scientific procedures or, for substances used in food
before 1958, through either scientific procedures or experience based on common use in food)
are unapproved food additives. In some cases, FDA has determined that a substance is not
GRAS for use as an ingredient in food (see, e.g., FDA’s memorandum “Regulatory status and
review of available information pertaining to tara protein/flour derived from the seed germ of the
plant, *Caesalpinia spinosa* : lack of general recognition of safety for its use in foods” (FDA,
2024b)). In other cases, FDA has determined that a process contaminant that forms above a
specified level in a food product during production causes the original ingredient to not be
GRAS and, therefore, it is an unsafe food additive (see, e.g., CPG 500.500, Guidance Levels for
3-MCPD (3-chloro-1,2-propanediol) in Acid-Hydrolyzed Protein and Asian-Style Sauces, Table 3
in section VI of the Introduction of this guidance). \[20\]
In evaluating whether the potential for an unapproved food additive or color additive is a hazard
requiring a preventive control, we recommend that you consider the resources we identified in
section 12.3.2 and factors we identified in section 12.3.4.

#### 12.3.10 Evaluating Biogenic Amines in Animal-derived Foods

The PCHF requirements specify that you must consider, as part of your hazard identification,
known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”) chemical hazards that include decomposition (see
21 CFR 117.130(b)(1)(ii)). Biogenic amines, such as histamine produced from the breakdown of
the amino acid histidine, are the most common example of a decomposition product. Biogenic
amines are most commonly associated with seafood (which is generally covered by the Seafood
HACCP regulation \[21\] and not covered by preventive controls requirements in part 117). In foods
other than seafood, biogenic amines are principally associated with certain cheeses (particularly
aged cheeses) and generally managed through practices that minimize the potential for growth
and histamine production by undesirable microorganisms.
In evaluating whether biogenic amines in a cheese product could be a hazard requiring a
preventive control, we recommend that you consider the factors we identified in section 12.3.4.
20 Note that we also discuss 3-MCPD as a process contaminant in acid-hydrolyzed protein and Asianstyle sauces in section 12.3.12, which discusses process contaminants more broadly.
21 21 CFR Part 123; Procedures for the Safe and Sanitary Processing and Importing of Fish and Fishery
Products (Seafood HACCP regulation).

#### 12.3.11 Evaluating Substances Introduced for Economic Gain

The PCHF requirements specify that you must consider, as part of your hazard identification,
known or reasonably foreseeable hazards that may be intentionally introduced for purposes of
economic gain (21 CFR 117.130(b)(2)(iii)).
In evaluating whether a chemical contaminant introduced for economic gain could be a hazard
requiring a preventive control, we recommend that you:

- consider the factors we identified in section 12.3.4; and
- focus on circumstances where there has been a pattern of such adulteration in the past,
suggesting a potential for intentional adulteration even though the past occurrences may not
be associated with the specific supplier or the specific food product. \[22\] For example:
`o` Lead salts have been illegally added to certain spices to increase their weight and
enhance their color, in an attempt to increase the monetary value of the adulterated
spices (Cowell et al., 2017). In 2023, FDA, along with CDC and state and local partners,
began investigating reports of elevated blood lead levels in individuals with reported
exposure to certain cinnamon-containing applesauce products (CDC, 2024).
Investigations pointed to cinnamon used in these products as the likely source of
contamination. In FDA’s testing of affected products and the cinnamon used in the
products, FDA found very high levels of lead and chromium and determined that the lead
and chromium are from lead chromate (FDA, 2024a). As of the date of this guidance,
FDA’s leading hypothesis is that this was likely an act of economically motivated
adulteration.
`o` Milk firms in one country added melamine, a nitrogen-rich industrial by-product, to
diluted dairy products to increase the apparent protein content (see Table 8 in section VI
of the Introduction of this guidance).
`o` The United Kingdom Food Standards Agency has documented a timeline (ranging from
May 2003 through February 2005) for adulterated chili products containing Sudan I, an
orange-red solid organic chemical, classified as an azo dye, that has carcinogenic
properties (United Kingdom Food Standards Agency, 2005).

#### 12.3.12 Evaluating Process-related Contaminants

##### 12.3.12.1 3-MCPDEs and GEs

The process-related chemical hazards 3-MCPDEs and GEs are contaminants that can occur in
edible oils and foods made from these oils (see Table 8 in section VI of the Introduction of this
guidance). \[23\] Refined oils are often a major component of infant formula. Following a risk
22 See the resources applicable to “food fraud” that we list in Table 8 in section VI of the Introduction of
this guidance. See also Import Alert 99-47 (Detention Without Physical Examination of Human Food
Products That Appear to be Adulterated for Economic Gain; Table 5 in section VI of the Introduction). In
addition, Table 3-8 in draft Chapter 3 of this guidance is a quick reference guide listing circumstances
where there has been a pattern of such adulteration in the past.
23 The draft Chapter 3 that we made available for public comment in 2016 did not discuss 3-MCPDE and

assessment by JECFA, the CAC, in which FDA participates, developed recommendations for
industry on reducing 3-MCPDE and GE in refined oils, particularly when used in infant formula
(see Table 6 in section VI of the Introduction). In evaluating 3-MCPDE and GE levels in refined
oils and foods that include refined oils as ingredients, FDA has focused much of its testing
efforts on infant formula because infants are a vulnerable population, infant formula contains
relatively large amounts of oil (about 25-30%) to support infants’ nutritional needs, and, for
some infants, infant formula is a sole food source. Because of the combined efforts of industry
and FDA, average 3-MCPDE and GE levels in infant formula in the United States have declined
over the last several years.
In evaluating whether 3-MCPDEs or GEs could be a hazard requiring a preventive control (e.g.,
a process control for a food that you manufacture, or a supply-chain control for a food that you
use as a raw material or other ingredient), we recommend that you consider:

- the factors identified in section 12.3.4; and
- the potential that your refined oil could be used as an ingredient in infant formula.

##### 12.3.12.2 3-MCPD in acid-hydrolyzed protein and Asian-style sauces

The process-related chemical hazard 3-MCPD \[24\] is a contaminant that can occur in acidhydrolyzed protein and Asian-style sauces (see section 12.3.9 and CPG Sec. 500.500; Table 3
in section VI of the Introduction of this guidance).

- Acid-hydrolyzed protein (acid-HP) is prepared by the hydrolysis of proteins by heat and
food-grade acids. During the production of acid-HP, the reaction of hydrochloric acid (HCl)
with residual fat in the protein starting material may form 3-MCPD, a member of a group of
chemicals known as chloropropanols, which have been identified as carcinogens. The
manufacturing process for acid-HP can be modified to reduce the levels of 3-MCPD that are
formed (see Codex Code of Practice for the Reduction of 3-Monochloropropane-1,2-Diol
During the Production of Acid-HVPs and Products That Contain Acid-HVPs, CXC 64-2008,
Table 6 in section VI of the Introduction of this guidance).
- Acid-HP can be added to soybeans and other ingredients to produce soy sauce that does
not undergo a traditional fermentation process, added to fermented sauces to enhance the
flavor of the sauce, and used as an ingredient in other Asian-style sauces. In some cases,
HCl may be added directly to soybeans to make soy sauce, so that acid-HP is formed during
production of the soy sauce. Adding HCl directly to soybeans can result in reactions with
residual fat to generate chloropropanols unless the processing conditions are well
controlled. A range of techniques can be used in the manufacture of soy sauces. Generally,
products made exclusively by means of fermentation do not contain chloropropanols, or, if
present, they only occur in trace amounts (see Codex Code of Practice for the Reduction of
3-Monochloropropane-1,2-Diol During the Production of Acid-HVPs and Products That
Contain Acid-HVPs, CXC 64-2008, Table 6 in section VI of the Introduction of this
guidance).
GE. When we finalize that chapter, we intend to reference the information on FDA’s website regarding 3MCPDE and GE.
24 Chemical names for 3-MCPD include 3-chloro-1,2-propanediol (as specified in CPG Sec. 500.500), 3monochloropropane-1,2-diol, and 3-chloropropane-1,2-diol.

In evaluating whether 3-MCPD is a hazard requiring a preventive control (e.g., a process control
for a food that you manufacture, or a supply-chain control for a food that you use as a raw
material or other ingredient), we recommend that you consider the factors identified in section
12.3.4.

##### 12.3.12.3 4-methylimidazole (4-MEI)

The chemical 4-MEI can form as a byproduct during the manufacturing of certain types of
caramel coloring (known as Class III and Class IV caramel coloring), which are commonly used
color additives. The results of toxicological studies conducted in rodents using levels of 4-MEI
that far exceed current estimates of human exposure to 4-MEI from the consumption of food
have shown that 4-MEI can cause adverse effects when present at high levels (NTP, 2007).
These studies include a 2-year study in rats (which was inconclusive regarding carcinogenicity),
a 2-year study in mice (which showed an increased incidence of certain lung tumors), and a
multi-generation reproductive and developmental study on 4-MEI in rats (which showed
reproductive and developmental effects in male and female rats) (see List of Select Chemicals
in the Food Supply Under FDA Review, Table 8 in section VI of the Introduction of this
guidance).
FDA is currently reviewing all available data on the safety of 4-MEI. In 2018, FDA published an
assessment of potential consumer exposure to 4-MEI from the use of Class III and Class IV
caramel coloring in food products (Folmer et al., 2018). FDA’s current review, along with this
exposure assessment, will help FDA determine what, if any, regulatory action needs to be
taken. Such actions could include setting a limit on the amount of 4-MEI that can be present in
Class III and IV caramel coloring.
In evaluating whether 4-MEI can be a hazard requiring a preventive control (e.g., a process
control for a food that you manufacture, or a supply-chain control for a food that you use as a
raw material or other ingredient), we recommend that you consider:

- the factors identified in section 12.3.4; and
- current information about manufacturing controls to reduce exposure to 4-MEI due to its
presence in Class III and IV caramel coloring.

##### 12.3.12.4 Acrylamide

The process-related chemical hazard acrylamide is formed during high-temperature cooking
processes (including frying, roasting, or baking) due to interaction between sugars and amino
acids that are naturally present in foods. Acrylamide is found mainly in foods made from plants,
including potato products, grain products, and coffee. Acrylamide in food is a concern because it
can cause cancer in laboratory animals at high doses and is “reasonably anticipated to be a
human carcinogen based on sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity from studies in experimental
animals” (National Toxicology Program, 2011). In 2010, an international evaluation of
acrylamide by JECFA concluded that acrylamide may be “a human health concern" (JECFA,
2011b). Reducing acrylamide levels in foods may mitigate potential human health risks from
exposure to acrylamide. For additional information about acrylamide and measures to reduce
acrylamide in food, see our “Acrylamide” website and “Fact Sheets” regarding reducing
acrylamide in cereal-based foods and in potato-based foods (see Table 8 in section VI of the
Introduction of this guidance).

### 12.4 Examples of Control Measures for Chemical Hazards

See also our “Guidance for Industry: Acrylamide in Foods” (Table 4 in section VI of the
Introduction of this guidance). In that guidance, we recommend that manufacturers evaluate
approaches to acrylamide reduction that may be relevant to their particular processes and
consider adopting approaches, if feasible, that reduce acrylamide levels in their products.
In evaluating whether acrylamide could be a hazard requiring a preventive control (e.g., a
process control for a food that you manufacture, or a supply-chain control for a food that you
use as a raw material or other ingredient), we recommend that you consider the factors we
identified in section 12.3.4.

#### 12.3.13 Evaluating Facility-related Chemicals

Facility-related chemical hazards such as cleaning chemicals have long been addressed
through application of CGMPs. We are not aware of circumstances in which these chemical
hazards would be a hazard requiring a preventive control.

##### **12.4 Examples of Control Measures for Chemical Hazards**

See Table 12-2 for examples of control measures for chemical hazards. As discussed in section
12.3.4, you determine through your hazard analysis whether a hazard can be effectively
managed through the application of control measures, such as CGMPs or other prerequisite
programs, or whether a hazard requires one or more preventive controls.

This chapter focuses on supply-chain programs for incoming raw materials and other
ingredients, and process controls that you identify and implement to produce your food product,
because these preventive controls are most relevant to chemical hazards requiring a preventive
control. Based on your hazard analysis, there may be other preventive controls to consider.
A food safety plan is facility specific. However, a corporation may designate an individual at the
corporate level as the owner, operator, or agent in charge of a particular facility, and an
employee of the corporation, whether at headquarters or at another facility owned by the

### 12.6 Identify and Implement a Process Control and Associated Preventive Control Management Components for a Chemical Hazard

corporation, may provide input into a particular facility’s food safety plan (80 FR 55908 at 56022,
September 17, 2015). Examples of aspects of a food safety plan for a chemical hazard that can
be handled at the corporate \[25\] level include:

- written procedures that will be included in the food safety plan (see section 12.8.1); and
- a supply-chain program for those raw materials and other ingredients for which a
manufacturing/processing facility has identified a chemical hazard that is controlled before
its receipt (see section 12.7 and Chapter 15 of this guidance).
Other aspects of a food safety plan for a chemical hazard are not suitable for handling at the
corporate level. For example, process controls and associated preventive control management
components (monitoring, verification, corrective actions and corrections, and associated
records) are conducted at an individual facility (see section 12.6).
In the remainder of this chapter, we discuss preventive controls for chemical hazards from the
perspective of an individual facility, without repeating within each discussion that certain aspects
of a food safety plan that includes preventive controls for chemical hazards could be handled at
the corporate level.
Part 117 requires that certain activities either be performed, or overseen by, a PCQI. When a
PCQI oversees (rather than performs) these activities, the activity could be performed by a
designee of the PCQI. For simplicity, when discussing the role of the PCQI within the examples
in this chapter we describe the activity as performed by a PCQI, without specifying each time
that the activity could be performed by a designee of the PCQI.

#### 12.6.1 Identify a Process Control

See Table 12-2 in section 12.4 for examples of control measures that you could identify and
implement as a process control for a chemical hazard.

#### 12.6.2 Develop a Strategy for Preventive Control Management Components

With some exceptions, part 117 specifies that preventive controls are subject to the following
preventive control management components as appropriate to ensure the effectiveness of the
preventive controls, taking into account the nature of the preventive control and its role in the
facility’s food safety system: (1) monitoring; (2) corrective actions and corrections; and (3)
verification \[26\] (see 21 CFR 117.140). We discuss each of these preventive control management
components as they relate to a process control for chemical hazards in section 12.6.3 through
12.6.5.
25 In some cases, programs handled by corporate are managed as prerequisite programs rather than as
preventive controls.
26 Verification includes validation (see 21 CFR 117.155(a)(1)).

#### 12.6.3 Design and Validation of a Process Control for a Chemical Hazard

With some exceptions, \[27\] part 117 requires that you validate that the preventive controls are
adequate to control the hazard as appropriate to the nature of the preventive control and its role
in your food safety system (see 21 CFR 117.160(a)). The validation of the preventive controls
must be performed (or overseen) by a PCQI (see 21 CFR 117.160(b)(1)). “Validation” means
obtaining and evaluating scientific and technical evidence that a control measure, combination
of control measures, or the food safety plan as a whole, when properly implemented, is capable
of effectively controlling the identified hazards (see 21 CFR 117.3).
In general, based on the nature of the preventive controls discussed in this chapter, the
validation of preventive controls for chemical hazards will involve approaches such as obtaining
scientific or technical information from credible sources and obtaining experimental data. This
could include collection of data during operating conditions (e.g., monitoring results,
measurements, test results) to support that process controls are scientifically sound, can
effectively control the chemical hazard, and function as intended on a day-to-day basis.

#### 12.6.4 Establish, Implement, and Document Monitoring and Verification for a Process Control

##### 12.6.4.1 Requirements for monitoring

Part 117 requires that, as appropriate to the nature of the preventive control and its role in your
food safety system, you establish and implement written procedures, including the frequency
with which they are to be performed, for monitoring the preventive control. You must monitor the
preventive controls with adequate frequency to provide assurance that they are consistently
performed (see 21 CFR 117.145).
What you monitor depends on the process control you have identified as a preventive control.
See Table 12-3 for examples of what you could monitor. In general, what you monitor could be
associated with:

- the food;
- the chemical hazard; or
- the processing equipment.

##### 12.6.4.2 Requirements for verification

Part 117 requires that verification activities include, as appropriate to the nature of the
preventive control and its role in your food safety system: (1) validation; (2) verification that
monitoring is being conducted; (3) verification that appropriate decisions about corrective
actions are being made; (4) verification of implementation and effectiveness; and (5) reanalysis
(see 21 CFR 117.155). See section 12.6.3 for a discussion of validating a process control for a
chemical hazard.
27 See the exceptions in 21 CFR 117.160(c). In general, the type of preventive controls that are validated
are process controls.

Part 117 also requires that you verify that the preventive controls are consistently implemented
and are effectively and significantly minimizing or preventing the hazards. To do so you must
conduct certain activities as appropriate to the facility, the food, and the nature of the preventive
control and its role in the facility’s food safety system (see 21 CFR 117.165(a)). Among the
verification activities listed, those most relevant to process controls for a chemical hazard are:

- calibration of process monitoring instruments and verification instruments (or checking them
for accuracy) (see 21 CFR 117.165(a)(1));
- product testing (see 21 CFR 117.165(a)(2)); and
- review of certain records by (or under the oversight of) a PCQI at specified intervals (which
depend on the record), to ensure that the records are complete, the activities reflected in the
records occurred in accordance with the food safety plan, the preventive controls are
effective, and appropriate decisions were made about corrective actions (see 21 CFR
117.165(a)(4)).
Part 117 also requires, as appropriate to the facility, the food, the nature of the hazard and
preventive control, and the role of the preventive control in the facility’s food safety system, that
you establish and implement written procedures for certain verification activities (see 21 CFR
117.165(b)). Among the written procedures listed, those most relevant to this chapter are:
- the method and frequency of calibrating process monitoring instruments and verification
instruments (or checking them for accuracy) (see 21 CFR 117.117.165(b)(1)); and
- product testing (see 21 CFR 117.165(b)(2)).

##### 12.6.4.3 Flexibility in complying with the requirements for monitoring and verification

The requirements for monitoring provide flexibility for you to establish and implement written
procedures for monitoring preventive controls as appropriate to the nature of the preventive
control and its role in your food safety system (see 21 CFR 117.145). Likewise, the
requirements for verification provide flexibility for you to conduct verification activities that are
appropriate to the facility, the food, and the nature of the preventive control and its role in the
facility’s food safety system (see 21 CFR 117.165). In some cases (such as instrument
calibration, product testing \[28\], and review of records), part 117 specifically identifies an activity as
a verification activity. In other cases (such as measurement of refrigeration temperature), part
117 mentions records of the activity as records of monitoring. However, part 117 does not
specifically mention all activities that could be conducted as a preventive control management
component for a preventive control, and some activities (such as visual observation) could be
classified as either monitoring or as verification. In light of the flexibility that part 117 provides for
monitoring and verification, it generally makes little difference whether you consider some
activities (such as visual observation) to be monitoring or verification for the purposes of your
process control as long as you comply with requirements applicable to monitoring or verification.
Regardless of what you call them, your preventive control management component(s) must be
appropriate to ensure the effectiveness of the preventive controls (see 21 CFR 117.140(a)).
28 In some cases, in-process testing of a batch can be classified as either monitoring or verification. For
example, continuous measurement of a batch for pH would generally be classified as monitoring, and
measurement of representative samples of a batch for pH could be classified as either monitoring or
verification.

##### 12.6.4.4 Examples of monitoring and verification activities for a process control for a chemical hazard

See Table 12-3 for examples of monitoring or verification activities that could apply to a control
measure that you identify and implement as a process control for a chemical hazard. Table 12-3
focuses on the examples of control measures for chemical hazards that we listed in Table 12-2
in section 12.4. The examples shown are not all-inclusive of the types of processes or the
methods for monitoring and verification and do not illustrate all the information that you could
include on Form 2-C (Process Controls) \[29\] if you classify the activity as monitoring. We
recommend that your procedures identify “who conducts the activity” (e.g., a line operator, QC
personnel, the vendor of equipment that is being calibrated, or laboratory personnel who have
the knowledge, skills, and experience to conduct analytical tests).
Part 117 identifies review of certain records within specified timeframes (see 21 CFR
117.165(a)(4) and section 12.6.4.2). Because review of records as a verification activity
generally would apply to any preventive control, we do not specify it for each listing in Table 123.
